body_md:
For a Schwartz function, $\langle X\rangle^{\frac12}u_0$ is again a Schwartz function, so condition (i) holds. Assume $\langle X\rangle u_0\in W^{r,1}$ with $r>\frac32$, and fix $r'\in(\frac32,r)$, so that $\langle X\rangle u_0\in B^{r'}_{1,1}$. Choose $s_1>0$ so small that $s_2:=\frac32-\frac{s_1}4$ satisfies $s_1+s_2<r'$; then $s_1+2s_2=3+\frac{s_1}2>3$. Since every $\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_l$ is bounded on $L^1$ uniformly in $(j,l)$ and $\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_l\Delta_m=0$ unless $\max(j,l)\le m+2$, we get
$$\begin{aligned}\sum_{j,l\ge0}2^{s_1j+s_2l}\|\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf\|_{L^1}&\lesssim\sum_{m\ge0}\Big(\sum_{j,l\le m+2}2^{s_1j+s_2l}\Big)\|\Delta_mf\|_{L^1}\\&\lesssim\sum_{m\ge0}2^{(s_1+s_2)m}\|\Delta_mf\|_{L^1},\end{aligned}$$
that is, $B^{s_1+s_2}_{1,1}\subset B^{s_1,s_2}_{1,1}$, and hence $\langle X\rangle u_0\in B^{s_1,s_2}_{1,1}$. Moreover $u_0\in L^2$, because $|u_0|\le|\langle X\rangle u_0|$ and $B^{r'}_{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^2)\subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for $r'\ge1$. Condition (ii) holds.

Finally, let $u_0(x,y)=\1_{[0,1]}(x)g(y)$ with $g\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$ real, and $F:=\langle X\rangle u_0=\1_{[0,1]}(x)H(x,y)$, where $H(x,y):=\langle X\rangle g(y)$ is smooth, with bounded derivatives on $[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}$, and supported in $\mathbb{R}\times\operatorname{supp} g$. Since $\Delta^y_l$ acts on $y$ only, $\Delta^y_lF=\1_{[0,1]}(x)\,\Delta^y_lH$, and since $H$ is smooth in $y$, for every $q\ge0$,
$$\int_\mathbb{R}\Big(\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|\Delta^y_lH(x,y)|+\int_0^1|\partial_x\Delta^y_lH(x,y)|\,dx\Big)dy\lesssim_q2^{-ql}.$$
The left-hand side bounds the integral in $y$ of the total variation of $x\mapsto\Delta^y_lF(x,y)$. For $j\ge1$, the symbol $\psi_j(\xi,0)/(i\xi)$ is the dilate of a fixed smooth function supported away from $0$, multiplied by $2^{1-j}$; hence its kernel has $L^1$ norm $O(2^{-j})$, and $\|\Delta^x_jG\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}\lesssim2^{-j}\|G'\|$ for every function $G$ of bounded variation on $\mathbb{R}$, where $\|G'\|$ is the total variation. Therefore $\|\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lF\|_{L^1}\lesssim_q2^{-j}2^{-ql}$, and $F\in B^{s_1,s_2}_{1,1}$ for every $0<s_1<1$ and $s_2>0$, for instance $(s_1,s_2)=(\frac34,\frac54)$, with $s_1+2s_2=\frac{13}4>3$. The datum $g(x)\1_{[0,1]}(y)$ is treated in the same way, with the roles of $x$ and $y$ exchanged and $(s_1,s_2)=(\frac32,\frac78)$, which satisfies $s_1+2s_2=\frac{13}4$. Both data are bounded with compact support, hence in $L^2$, and condition (ii) holds.

For nonnegative quantities $f,g$ we write $f\lesssim g$ if $f\le Cg$ for a constant $C>0$ which does not depend on the variables and parameters under consideration, $f\gtrsim g$ if $g\lesssim f$, and $f\sim g$ if $f\lesssim g\lesssim f$; the dependence of $C$ on fixed quantities is indicated by a subscript when it matters. Constants may change from line to line. We write $f=O(g)$ if $|f|\lesssim g$, and $f=o(g)$ if $|f|/g$ tends to zero in the limit under consideration. For $z\in\mathbb{R}^d$ or $z\in\mathbb{C}$, $\langle z\rangle:=(1+|z|^2)^{1/2}$. We write $X=(x,y)$, $dX=dx\,dy$, $\|f\|_{L^p}$ for the norm of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^2)$, $\|c\|_{W^{r,\infty}}:=\sum_{|\gamma|\le r}\|\partial^\gamma c\|_{L^\infty}$ for integers $r\ge0$, and
$$\|f\|_{L^q_yL^p_x}:=\Big\|\,y\mapsto\|f(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R})}\Big\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R})}.$$
The $L^2$ pairing is $(f,g):=\int f\overline g\,dX$, and $\rightharpoonup$ denotes weak convergence in $L^2$. For $h\in\mathbb{R}^2$, $\tau_hf(X):=f(X+h)$ and $\delta_hf:=\tau_hf-f$; for $h\in\mathbb{R}$, $\delta^x_hf(x,y):=f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)$ and $\delta^y_hf(x,y):=f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)$. On the spectral side, $k=k_1+ik_2\in\mathbb{C}$, $dA(k)=dk_1dk_2$, $\nabla_k=(\partial_{k_1},\partial_{k_2})$, $\mathbb{C}^\pm:=\{\pm k_2>0\}$, and for a function $f$ on $\mathbb{C}^\pm$ we write $f^\pm(k_1):=\lim_{k_2\to0^\pm}f(k_1+ik_2)$ for its one-sided traces on $\mathbb{R}$, when they exist. $C_b(\mathbb{C})$ is the space of bounded continuous functions and $C_0(\mathbb{C})$ the space of continuous functions tending to zero at infinity, both with the supremum norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$; for measurable functions, $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the essential supremum. For $E\subset\mathbb{C}$ and $0<\alpha\le1$, we write
$$\|f\|_{C^\alpha(E)}:=\sup_E|f|+\sup\Big\{\frac{|f(k)-f(k')|}{|k-k'|^\alpha}:\ k,k'\in E,\ 0<|k-k'|\le1\Big\},$$
and $\|f\|_{C^\alpha}:=\|f\|_{C^\alpha(\mathbb{C})}$. $D(k_0,r)$ is the open disc of center $k_0$ and radius $r$. Finally, we fix a radial function $\vartheta\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}^2)$ with $0\le\vartheta\le1$, $\vartheta=1$ on $D(0,1)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\vartheta\subset D(0,2)$, and a radial nonnegative function $\varrho\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}^2)$ supported in $D(0,1)$ with $\int\varrho=1$, and we set $\varrho_\varepsilon:=\varepsilon^{-2}\varrho(\cdot/\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. We use $\vartheta$ and $\varrho$ both on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and on $\mathbb{C}\simeq\mathbb{R}^2$, and $\vartheta(s):=\vartheta(s,0)$ for $s\in\mathbb{R}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Proof of (i). Fix $k$ and $0<|h|\le\frac12$, and split $\mathbb{C}$ into $E_1=D(k,2|h|)$, $E_2=D(k,2)\setminus E_1$ and $E_3=\mathbb{C}\setminus D(k,2)$. On $E_1$ we bound the two kernels separately: since $E_1\subset D(k+h,3|h|)$,
$$\int_{E_1}\frac{dA(k')}{|k+h-k'|}\le\int_{D(k+h,3|h|)}\frac{dA(k')}{|k+h-k'|}=6\pi|h|,\quad \int_{E_1}\frac{dA(k')}{|k-k'|}=4\pi|h| .$$
On $E_2\cup E_3$ we have $|k+h-k'|\ge\frac12|k-k'|$, and each of the two differences of kernels below is bounded by $\frac{|h|}{|k+h-k'||k-k'|}$, hence
$$\Big|\frac1{k+h-k'}-\frac1{k-k'}\Big|+\Big|\frac1{|k+h-k'|}-\frac1{|k-k'|}\Big|\le\frac{4|h|}{|k-k'|^2}.$$
On $E_2$, the integral of this bound is at most $4|h|\int_{2|h|}^2\frac{2\pi r\,dr}{r^2}=8\pi|h|\log\frac1{|h|}$. On $E_3$, $\frac{4|h|}{|k-k'|^2}\le\frac{2|h|}{|k-k'|}$, and the integral against $|f|$ is at most $2\pi|h|\mathcal{I}|f|(k)$. Summing the three contributions and using $1\le\frac{1}{\log2}\log\frac1{|h|}$ gives \eqref{cauchymodulus}, and in particular the continuity of $\mathcal{C} f$ and $\mathcal{I}|f|$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Proof of (ii). The function $\frac1{\pi k}$ is locally integrable and $\bar\partial\frac1{\pi k}=\delta_0$, so that, for a test function $\varphi$ and $k'\in\mathbb{C}$, the Cauchy--Pompeiu formula gives
$$\varphi(k')=-\frac1\pi\int_\mathbb{C}\frac{\bar\partial\varphi(k)}{k-k'}\,dA(k).$$
Fubini's theorem is legitimate, since
$$\int_\mathbb{C}\int_\mathbb{C}\frac{|f(k')||\bar\partial\varphi(k)|}{|k-k'|}\,dA(k')\,dA(k)=\pi\int_\mathbb{C}|\bar\partial\varphi|\,\mathcal{I}|f|\,dA<\infty,$$
and it gives
$$\int_\mathbb{C}\mathcal{C} f\,(-\bar\partial\varphi)\,dA=\int_\mathbb{C} f(k')\Big(-\frac1\pi\int_\mathbb{C}\frac{\bar\partial\varphi(k)}{k-k'}dA(k)\Big)dA(k')=\int_\mathbb{C} f\varphi\,dA,$$
that is, $\bar\partial\mathcal{C} f=f$. If now $v\in C_0$ and $\bar\partial v=f$, then $v-\mathcal{C} f$ is continuous by (i) and $\bar\partial(v-\mathcal{C} f)=0$. By Weyl's lemma it is an entire function, and it tends to zero at infinity since $|\mathcal{C} f|\le\mathcal{I}|f|\in C_0$. By Liouville's theorem, $v=\mathcal{C} f$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Proof of (iii). Among all sets of area $\pi r^2$, the integral of the radially decreasing function $|k-k'|^{-1}$ is maximal on $D(k,r)$, so that $\mathcal{I}\1_D(k)\le\frac1\pi\int_{D(k,r)}\frac{dA(k')}{|k-k'|}=2r$. For the rectangle $Q=I_1\times I_2$ with $|I_1|=L_1\ge L_2=|I_2|$, we use the disc bound on $D(k,L_2)$, and on $Q\setminus D(k,L_2)$ we use $|k-k'|\ge\max(L_2,|k_1-k_1'|)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{Q\setminus D(k,L_2)}\frac{dA(k')}{|k-k'|}&\le L_2\int_{I_1}\frac{dk_1'}{\max(L_2,|k_1-k'_1|)}\\&\le 2L_2\int_0^{L_1}\frac{ds}{\max(L_2,s)}=2L_2\Big(1+\log\frac{L_1}{L_2}\Big);\end{aligned}$$
the case $L_1\le L_2$ is symmetric. Finally, if $g=0$, the last bound and the assertion $\mathcal{I} g\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$ are immediate. Assume $g\neq0$. Splitting the potential at distance $r>0$ from $k$,
$$\mathcal{I} g(k)\le\frac1\pi\|g\|_\infty\int_{D(k,r)}\frac{dA(k')}{|k-k'|}+\frac1{\pi r}\int_{\{|k-k'|\ge r\}}g\,dA\le2r\|g\|_\infty+\frac{\|g\|_{L^1}}{\pi r},$$
and the choice $r=(\|g\|_{L^1}/(2\pi\|g\|_\infty))^{\frac12}$ gives the last bound of \eqref{potentialsets}. Applying it to $g\1_{\{|k'|>R\}}$ shows that $\mathcal{I}(g\1_{\{|k'|>R\}})$ is uniformly small for $R$ large, while $\mathcal{I}(g\1_{\{|k'|\le R\}})(k)\le\frac{\|g\|_{L^1}}{\pi(|k|-R)}$ for $|k|>R$. Since $\mathcal{I} g$ is continuous by (i), $\mathcal{I} g\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Proof of (iv) and (v). If $|k|\le\frac R2$ and $|k'|>R$, then $|k-k'|\ge\frac12|k'|$, so that
$$\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k'|>R\}})(k)\le\frac2\pi\int_{\{|k'|>R\}}\frac{F(k')}{|k'|}\,dA(k')\longrightarrow0\quad(R\to\infty),$$
because $\frac1\pi\int\frac{F(k')}{|k'|}dA(k')=\mathcal{I} F(0)<\infty$. If $|k|>\frac R2$, then $\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k'|>R\}})(k)\le\mathcal{I} F(k)\le\sup_{|k''|>R/2}\mathcal{I} F(k'')$, which tends to zero since $\mathcal{I} F\in C_0$. This proves the first claim of (iv). If $0\le G\le F$, then $G\1_{D(0,R)}\in L^1\cap L^\infty$, so that $\mathcal{I}(G\1_{D(0,R)})\in C_0$ by (iii), while $\mathcal{I}(G\1_{\{|k'|\ge R\}})\le\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k'|\ge R\}})$ is uniformly small for $R$ large; hence $\mathcal{I} G$ is a uniform limit of functions of $C_0(\mathbb{C})$, and $\mathcal{I} G\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$. If $F$ is bounded, the strip $\{|k_2'|<\varepsilon,\ |k'|\le R\}$ is contained in a rectangle with sides $2R$ and $2\varepsilon$, so that, by \eqref{potentialsets},
$$\sup_k\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k_2'|<\varepsilon\}})(k)\le\sup_k\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k'|>R\}})(k)+C\|F\|_\infty\,\varepsilon\Big(1+\log\frac R\varepsilon\Big).$$
Choosing first $R$ large and then $\varepsilon$ small proves the first claim of (v). For the second one, we split $\mathbb{C}$ into $\{|k'|>R\}$, $\{|k_2'|<\varepsilon,|k'|\le R\}$ and the compact set $K_{R,\varepsilon}=\{|k'|\le R,|k_2'|\ge\varepsilon\}$: by \eqref{potentialsets},
$$\|\mathcal{I}|f_n|\|_\infty\le\sup_k\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k'|>R\}})(k)+\sup_k\mathcal{I}(F\1_{\{|k_2'|<\varepsilon\}})(k)+2R\sup_{K_{R,\varepsilon}}|f_n|,$$
and we let $n\to\infty$, then $\varepsilon\to0$ and $R\to\infty$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 5:} Proof of (vi). Since $\bar\partial\phi$ is continuous and does not vanish on the support of $f$, the function $\frac f{\bar\partial\phi}$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb{C}$, and so is $g:=\frac{e^{i\phi}f}{i\bar\partial\phi}\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$. Since $\bar\partial e^{i\phi}=i(\bar\partial\phi)e^{i\phi}$,
$$\bar\partial g=e^{i\phi}f+e^{i\phi}\,\bar\partial\Big(\frac f{i\bar\partial\phi}\Big)\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb{C}),$$
so that $\mathcal{I}|\bar\partial g|\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$ by (iii), and (ii) gives $g=\mathcal{C}(\bar\partial g)$, which is \eqref{ibp}.

label: similarity
title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Local regularity and the similarity principle. Let $f$ be as in (i) and let $v\in C_0$ satisfy $\bar\partial v=a\overline v+f$ in $\mathcal D'$. On a disc $D(k_0,r)$, the function $v-\mathcal{C}(\1_{D(k_0,2r)}(a\overline v+f))$ is holomorphic in $D(k_0,2r)$, and $\partial_k\mathcal{C}$ is the Beurling transform, which is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$ by the Calder\'on--Zygmund theory \cite{Stein}; hence $v\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ for every $p\in(2,\infty)$. We claim that
\begin{equation}
\label{similarity}
v=e^{\sigma}\,\mathcal{C}(e^{-\sigma}f),\qquad \sigma:=\mathcal{C}\tilde a,\qquad \tilde a:=\begin{cases}a\overline v/v&\mbox{on}\ \{v\neq0\},\\ 0&\mbox{on}\ \{v=0\},\end{cases}
\end{equation}
which implies \eqref{pointwisevekua}, since $|\tilde a|\le|a|$ gives $|\sigma|\le\mathcal{I}|a|\le M$, hence $|e^{\pm\sigma}|\le e^M$. By construction $\tilde av=a\overline v$ almost everywhere. By Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy}, $\sigma$ is continuous and $\bar\partial\sigma=\tilde a$, and $\sigma\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ as above. Hence the product rule applies and
$$\bar\partial(e^{-\sigma}v)=e^{-\sigma}(\bar\partial v-\tilde av)=e^{-\sigma}f .$$
The function $e^{-\sigma}v-\mathcal{C}(e^{-\sigma}f)$ belongs to $C_0$, because $|e^{-\sigma}v|\le e^M|v|$ and $|\mathcal{C}(e^{-\sigma}f)|\le e^M\mathcal{I}|f|$, and it is $\bar\partial$-closed. By Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (ii) it vanishes, which proves \eqref{similarity}.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Compactness. Let $\mathcal Tv:=\mathcal{C}(a\overline v)$; it is a real-linear operator on the real Banach space $C_0(\mathbb{C})$. If $\|v\|_\infty\le1$, then $|\mathcal Tv|\le\mathcal{I}|a|$, and by \eqref{cauchymodulus} the family $\{\mathcal Tv\}$ has the common modulus of continuity $C|h|\log\frac1{|h|}(\|a\|_\infty+M)$. Since $\mathcal{I}|a|\in C_0$, the family is moreover uniformly small outside large discs. By the Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem, $\mathcal T$ is compact on $C_0(\mathbb{C})$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Proof of (i). If $v\in C_0$ and $v=\mathcal Tv$, then $\bar\partial v=a\overline v$ by Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (ii), and \eqref{similarity} with $f=0$ gives $v=0$. Thus $I-\mathcal T$ is injective, and the Fredholm alternative for compact operators on real Banach spaces shows that $I-\mathcal T$ is invertible on $C_0(\mathbb{C})$. Since $\mathcal{C} f\in C_0$ by Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (i) and $|\mathcal{C} f|\le\mathcal{I}|f|$, the function $v:=(I-\mathcal T)^{-1}\mathcal{C} f$ is the unique solution of \eqref{eqvekua} in $C_0$. It satisfies $\bar\partial v=a\overline v+f$, so that \eqref{pointwisevekua} follows from Step 1. Finally, if $v'\in C_0$ and $\bar\partial v'=a\overline{v'}+f$, then $w:=v'-v\in C_0$ satisfies $\bar\partial w=a\overline w$, and \eqref{similarity} with $f=0$ gives $w=0$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Proof of (ii) and (iii). Let $b\in C_b$. If $v\in C_b$ solves $v=b+\mathcal Tv$, then $w:=v-b=\mathcal{C}(a\overline b)+\mathcal{C}(a\overline w)$ belongs to $C_0$, because $\mathcal{C}(a\overline v)$ is continuous by Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (i) and bounded by $\|v\|_\infty\mathcal{I}|a|\in C_0$. Conversely, (i) with $f:=a\overline b$, for which $\mathcal{I}|f|\le\|b\|_\infty\mathcal{I}|a|\in C_0$, provides a unique such $w$, with
$$|w(k)|\le e^{2M}\mathcal{I}|a\overline b|(k)\le e^{2M}\|b\|_\infty\,\mathcal{I}|a|(k)\le Me^{2M}\|b\|_\infty .$$
This proves (iii), and (ii) is the case $b=1$. When $b$ is constant, $w\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ by Step 1, and so is $v=b+w$; together with Step 1, this proves (v).\\

\noindent{\bf Step 5:} Proof of (iv). Subtracting the equations of $m_1$ and $m_2$ gives
$$m_1-m_2=\mathcal{C}\big((a_1-a_2)\overline{m_2}\big)+\mathcal{C}\big(a_1\overline{(m_1-m_2)}\big).$$
This is \eqref{eqvekua} with $a=a_1$ and $f=(a_1-a_2)\overline{m_2}$, so that \eqref{pointwisevekua} and \eqref{boundeigen} give
$|m_1-m_2|\le e^{2M_1}\|m_2\|_\infty\,\mathcal{I}|a_1-a_2|\le e^{2M_1}(1+M_2e^{2M_2})\|\mathcal{I}|a_1-a_2|\|_\infty$.

title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Bounds and symmetry. By \eqref{hypa}, $|a|\lesssim\langle \zeta\rangle^{-6}$, and Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (ii), together with Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (iv), gives $\mathcal{I}|a|\in C_0$ and $\mathcal{I}(|k_2a|)\in C_0$. Since $|aP|=|a|$, Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (ii) applied to the coefficient $aP$ gives the unique solution $m$ and the bound of (i), uniformly in $(t,X)$. By Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (ii), $\bar\partial m=aP\overline m$, hence $\bar\partial m^*=a^*P^*\overline{m^*}=aP\overline{m^*}$, because $a^*=a$ and $P^*=P$. Since $m^*-1\in C_0$, the uniqueness part of Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (i), applied to $v'=m^*-1$ and $f=aP$, gives $m^*=m$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Derivatives in $x$. Let $f:=-2ik_2aP\overline m$. Then $\mathcal{I}|f|$ is bounded by $2\|m\|_\infty\mathcal{I}(|k_2a|)$, which belongs to $C_0$. Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (i) provides a unique solution $w\in C_0$ of the equation $w=\mathcal{C}(aP\overline w)+\mathcal{C} f$, and
$$|w(k)|\le e^{2M}\mathcal{I}|f|(k)\le2e^{2M}\|m\|_\infty\,\mathcal{I}(|k_2a|)(k)\lesssim\langle k\rangle^{-1}$$
by Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (ii). We show that $w=\partial_xm$. For $h\neq0$, let $P_h:=P(\cdot;t,x+h,y)$ and $q_h:=h^{-1}\delta^x_hm(\cdot;t,X)$. Subtracting the equations \eqref{eqm} at $x+h$ and at $x$, we find that $q_h-w$ solves
$$\begin{aligned}q_h-w&=\mathcal{C}\big(aP_h\overline{(q_h-w)}\big)+b_h,\\ b_h&:=\mathcal{C}\big(a(P_h-P)\overline w\big)+\mathcal{C}\Big(a\Big(\frac{P_h-P}h+2ik_2P\Big)\overline m\Big).\end{aligned}$$
Now $\frac{P_h-P}h=\frac{e^{-2ik_2h}-1}hP$ is bounded by $2|k_2|$ and converges to $-2ik_2P$ uniformly on compact sets as $h\to0$. Since $|k_2a|$ is bounded and $\mathcal{I}(|k_2a|)\in C_0$, Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (v) gives $\|b_h\|_\infty\to0$, and Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (iii) gives $\|q_h-w\|_\infty\le(1+Me^{2M})\|b_h\|_\infty\to0$. Thus $\partial_xm=w$ in $C_b(\mathbb{C})$, which proves \eqref{eqmx} and the bound on $\partial_xm$. Differentiating \eqref{eqmx} in the same way, $\partial_x^2m$ is the solution in $C_0$ of
$$\partial_x^2m=\mathcal{C}(aP\overline{\partial_x^2m})+\mathcal{C}\big(-4ik_2aP\overline{\partial_xm}-4k_2^2aP\overline m\big),$$
whose source is bounded by $C(|k_2|+k_2^2)|a|$. By \eqref{pointwisevekua} and \eqref{weightsE}, $|\partial_x^2m(k)|\lesssim\mathcal{I}\big((|k_2|+k_2^2)\langle \zeta\rangle^{-6}\big)(k)\lesssim\langle k\rangle^{-1}$. The same comparison argument, based on Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (v) and Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (iii), shows that $m$, $\partial_xm$ and $\partial_x^2m$ depend continuously on $(t,X)$ in $C_b(\mathbb{C})$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} The reconstruction. We have
$$\begin{gathered}\partial_x(aP\overline m)=aP\big(-2ik_2\overline m+\overline{\partial_xm}\big),\\ \partial_x^2(aP\overline m)=aP\big(-4k_2^2\overline m-4ik_2\overline{\partial_xm}+\overline{\partial_x^2m}\big).\end{gathered}$$
By (i), (ii) and \eqref{hypa}, both are bounded by $C(|k_2|+k_2^2+\langle k\rangle^{-1})\langle \zeta\rangle^{-6}$, which is integrable by \eqref{weightsE}. Hence \eqref{reconstruction} converges absolutely, we may differentiate under the integral sign, and $u$ and $\partial_xu$ are bounded and, by Step 2 and dominated convergence, continuous. By Step 1, the integrand of \eqref{reconstruction} is invariant under $g\mapsto g^*$, so that the change of variables $k\mapsto\bar k$ shows that the integral is real: $u$ is real-valued. Finally, \eqref{freespectral} applies since $k_2a\in L^1$, and \eqref{remainder} follows.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Proof of (iv). By Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (v), $m$ and $\partial_xm$ belong to $W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$, and by Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (ii), \eqref{eqm} and \eqref{eqmx} give $\bar\partial m=aP\overline m$ and $\bar\partial\partial_xm=aP\overline{\partial_xm}-2ik_2aP\overline m$. Taking complex conjugates, $\partial_k\overline m=\overline{aP}\,m$ and $\partial_k\overline{\partial_xm}=\overline{aP}\,\partial_xm+2ik_2\overline{aP}\,m$. Since $\partial_k(-2ik_2)=-1$, we obtain
$$\partial_kB=-\overline{(m-1)}-2ik_2\overline{aP}\,m+\overline{aP}\,\partial_xm+2ik_2\overline{aP}\,m,$$
which is \eqref{cancellation}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\hat\varphi\in C^\infty_c(\{\xi\neq0\})$ and let $V$ be as in Lemma \ref{lemmafree}. Since $S(t)$ is unitary,
$$\big(S(-t)u(t)-g,\varphi\big)=\big(u(t)-S(t)g,S(t)\varphi\big)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\big(u_n(t)-S(t)g_n,S(t)\varphi\big)$$
for every fixed $t$. We split the last pairing into the integrals over $\{X/t\in V\}$ and over its complement. By \eqref{hypcone} and \eqref{freecones}, the first one is bounded by
$$\sup_n\sup_{X/t\in V}|u_n(t,X)-S(t)g_n(X)|\ \|S(t)\varphi\|_{L^1}=o(|t|^{-1})\cdot O(|t|)=o(1),$$
and by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and \eqref{freecones} the second one is bounded by $\sup_n(\|u_n(t)\|_{L^2}+\|g_n\|_{L^2})\|\1_{\{X/t\notin V\}}S(t)\varphi\|_{L^2}=o(1)$, both uniformly in $n$. Hence $(S(-t)u(t)-g,\varphi)\to0$ as $t\to\pm\infty$. The functions $\varphi$ with $\hat\varphi\in C^\infty_c(\{\xi\neq0\})$ are dense in $L^2$, and $S(-t)u(t)$ is bounded in $L^2$, so that $S(-t)u(t)\rightharpoonup g$. If $\|S(-t)u(t)\|_{L^2}=\|u(t)\|_{L^2}=\|g\|_{L^2}$, the weak convergence, together with the convergence of the norms, implies the strong convergence in $L^2$.

head: environment
name: Spatial decay and analyticity in the amplitude

title: Proof
body_md:
If $b=0$, take $\mathcal U=\mathbb{C}$, $m_s=n_s=1$ and $W_s=0$; all assertions are immediate. We henceforth assume $b\neq0$.

{\bf Step 1:} Solvability. Let $\mathcal T(m,n):=\big(\mathcal{C}(bP_0n),\overline{\mathcal{C}}(\overline bP_0^{-1}m)\big)$. It is a complex-linear operator on $C_b(\mathbb{C})^2$, with norm at most $M:=\|\mathcal{I}|b|\|_\infty$ independently of $X$, since $|P_0|=1$. Let $s_0\in\mathbb{R}$. For data of the form $(G,\overline G)$, $G\in C_b$, the equation $(I-s_0\mathcal T)(m,n)=(G,\overline G)$ is solved by $(v,\overline v)$, where $v$ is the solution of $v=G+\mathcal{C}(s_0bP_0\overline v)$ given by Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (iii): indeed $\overline{\overline\mathcal{C}(\overline bP_0^{-1}v)}=\mathcal{C}(bP_0\overline v)$. Every pair $(H_1,H_2)\in C_b^2$ is the combination $(G_1,\overline{G_1})+i(G_2,\overline{G_2})$ with $G_1=\frac12(H_1+\overline{H_2})$ and $G_2=\frac1{2i}(H_1-\overline{H_2})$, and the same decomposition applied to a solution of the homogeneous equation shows that it vanishes. Hence $I-s_0\mathcal T$ is invertible on $C_b^2$, with $\|(I-s_0\mathcal T)^{-1}\|\le\Lambda(s_0):=2(1+|s_0|Me^{2|s_0|M})$. For $|s-s_0|<r(s_0):=(4M\Lambda(s_0))^{-1}$ the Neumann series
$$(I-s\mathcal T)^{-1}=\sum_{j\ge0}(s-s_0)^j\big[(I-s_0\mathcal T)^{-1}\mathcal T\big]^j(I-s_0\mathcal T)^{-1}$$
converges, is holomorphic in $s$, and has norm at most $2\Lambda(s_0)$. We set $\mathcal U:=\bigcup_{s_0\in\mathbb{R}}D(s_0,r(s_0))$, which depends on $b$ only through $M$. A compact set $\mathcal U'\subset\mathcal U$ is covered by finitely many of these discs, so that $(I-s\mathcal T)^{-1}$ is bounded on $\mathcal U'$ uniformly in $X$. We define $(m_s,n_s):=(I-s\mathcal T)^{-1}(1,1)$. Since $\mathcal T$ maps $C_b^2$ into $C_0^2$, $m_s-1$ and $n_s-1$ belong to $C_0$. For real $s$ the data $(1,1)$ are of the form $(G,\overline G)$, so that $n_s=\overline{m_s}$.

Differentiating \eqref{system} in $X$ as in Step 2 of the proof of Lemma \ref{lemmainverse}, we see that $(\partial^\gamma_Xm_s,\partial^\gamma_Xn_s)=(I-s\mathcal T)^{-1}(G_\gamma)$, where the data $G_\gamma$ are combinations of lower-order derivatives multiplied by the bounded functions $(i\zeta(k))^\nu$, $k\in\operatorname{supp} b$, and of the powers of $s$. By induction, all these derivatives are bounded on $\mathbb{C}$, uniformly in $X$ and $s\in\mathcal U'$, and holomorphic in $s$. Differentiating under the integral sign, $\partial^\gamma_XW_s(X)$ is holomorphic in $s$ and $|\partial^\gamma_XW_s(X)|\lesssim|s|$, which proves \eqref{decayW} for $|X|\le1$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Approximate solution for $|X|\ge1$. Recall $\Gamma=\bar\partial_k(X\cdot\zeta(k))=-i(x+2\overline ky)$, so that $\bar\partial P_0=i\Gamma P_0$ and $\partial_kP_0^{-1}=-i\overline\Gamma P_0^{-1}$. If $|k_2|\ge\delta$ and $|k|\le\delta^{-1}$, then $|\Gamma|\gtrsim_\delta|X|$: when $|y|\ge\varepsilon|X|$ we use $|\operatorname{Im}(x+2\overline ky)|=2|k_2||y|$, and when $|y|\le\varepsilon|X|$ we use $|x+2k_1y|\ge(1-\varepsilon-2\varepsilon\delta^{-1})|X|$, with $\varepsilon$ small. Hence on $\operatorname{supp} b$, every derivative in $k$ of $\Gamma^{-1}$ is $O(|X|^{-1})$, and every derivative in $X$ of $\Gamma^{-1}$ gains one more power of $|X|^{-1}$. We set
$$g:=\frac b{i\Gamma},\qquad \tilde g:=\frac{\overline b}{-i\overline\Gamma},\qquad q:=\mathcal{C}(b\tilde g),\qquad \tilde q:=\overline{\mathcal{C}}(\overline bg),$$
$$m_{\rm app}:=1+sP_0\,g+s^2q,\qquad n_{\rm app}:=1+sP_0^{-1}\tilde g+s^2\tilde q .$$
The functions $g,\tilde g$ are smooth, supported in $\operatorname{supp} b$, and all their derivatives in $k$ are $O(|X|^{-1})$; since $b\tilde g$ and $\overline bg$ are smooth with compact support, the functions $q$ and $\tilde q$ are smooth on $\mathbb{C}$, and all their derivatives in $k$ are $O(|X|^{-1})$ as well. A direct computation, in which the terms $sbP_0$ and $s^2b\tilde g$ cancel in the first line and $s\overline bP_0^{-1}$ and $s^2\overline bg$ cancel in the second line, gives
$$\bar\partial m_{\rm app}-sbP_0n_{\rm app}=sP_0\,h,\qquad \partial_kn_{\rm app}-s\overline bP_0^{-1}m_{\rm app}=sP_0^{-1}\tilde h,$$
with $h:=\bar\partial g-s^2b\tilde q$ and $\tilde h:=\partial_k\tilde g-s^2\overline bq$, smooth functions supported in $\operatorname{supp} b$ whose derivatives are $O(|X|^{-1})$. Oscillation gains one more power: Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (vi), applied with the phase $X\cdot\zeta(k)$, whose $\bar\partial$-derivative is $\Gamma$, and \eqref{potentialsets} give
\begin{equation}
\label{gain}
\|\mathcal{C}(P_0h)\|_\infty\le\Big\|\frac h{\Gamma}\Big\|_\infty+\Big\|\mathcal{I}\Big|\bar\partial\frac h{\Gamma}\Big|\Big\|_\infty\lesssim|X|^{-2},
\end{equation}
and similarly $\|\overline\mathcal{C}(P_0^{-1}\tilde h)\|_\infty=\|\mathcal{C}(P_0\overline{\tilde h})\|_\infty\lesssim|X|^{-2}$. Since $m_{\rm app}-1$ and $n_{\rm app}-1$ belong to $C_0$, Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (ii) gives $(I-s\mathcal T)(m_{\rm app},n_{\rm app})=(1,1)+s\big(\mathcal{C}(P_0h),\overline\mathcal{C}(P_0^{-1}\tilde h)\big)$, hence
\begin{equation}
\label{errorapp}
\|m_s-m_{\rm app}\|_\infty+\|n_s-n_{\rm app}\|_\infty\lesssim|s||X|^{-2}.
\end{equation}
Differentiating in $X$ the equation satisfied by $(m_s-m_{\rm app},n_s-n_{\rm app})$, and applying \eqref{gain} to the differentiated amplitudes, the same bound holds for all derivatives in $X$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Decay of $W_s$. Inserting $n_{\rm app}$ in the definition of $W_s$ and using \eqref{errorapp},
$$W_s=s\int_\mathbb{C} bP_0\,dA+s^2J(X)+s^3\int_\mathbb{C} bP_0\tilde q\,dA+O(|s||X|^{-2}),$$
where $J(X):=\int_\mathbb{C}\frac{|b|^2}{-i\overline\Gamma}\,dA$.
By the change of variables \eqref{changevariables}, $\int bP_0\,dA$ is the Fourier transform of the function $\frac{b\circ\zeta^{-1}}{8|k_2|}\in C^\infty_c(\{\xi\neq0\})$, hence it decays faster than every power of $\langle X\rangle$. Integrating by parts once with $P_0=\frac{\bar\partial P_0}{i\Gamma}$, the third term is $O(|X|^{-2})$. Finally $|J(X)|\lesssim|X|^{-1}$, and each derivative in $X$ of $J$ gains a factor $|X|^{-1}$, because $\overline\Gamma$ is linear in $X$ and $|\overline\Gamma|\gtrsim|X|$ on $\operatorname{supp} b$. The same expansion holds for the derivatives in $X$, with the same bounds on the error terms. This proves \eqref{decayW} for $|X|\ge1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h:=u_1-u_2$. Since the nonlinear terms $u_j\partial_xu_j$ belong to $L^\infty([0,T];L^2)$, the function
$$S(-t)h(t)=-6\int_0^tS(-t')\big(u_1\partial_xu_1-u_2\partial_xu_2\big)(t')\,dt'$$
is absolutely continuous with values in $L^2$, and for almost every $t$
$$\frac d{dt}\|h\|_{L^2}^2=-12\big(h,u_1\partial_xu_1-u_2\partial_xu_2\big)=-12\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\big(h^2\partial_xu_1+u_2h\partial_xh\big)dX .$$
The function $u_2h^2$ and its derivative $(\partial_xu_2)h^2+2u_2h\partial_xh$ are integrable, because $u_2,h\in L^2\cap L^\infty$ and $\partial_xu_2,\partial_xh\in L^\infty$; hence, for almost every $y$, $x\mapsto u_2h^2$ belongs to $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$, and $\int u_2h\partial_xh\,dX=-\frac12\int(\partial_xu_2)h^2\,dX$. Therefore $\frac d{dt}\|h\|_{L^2}^2\le12\big(\|\partial_xu_1\|_{L^\infty}+\|\partial_xu_2\|_{L^\infty}\big)\|h\|_{L^2}^2$, and Gronwall's lemma gives $h=0$.

label: propplancherel
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Nonlinear Plancherel identity for compactly supported coefficients

title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Weak scattering. The single coefficient $a$ satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{propcone} with $F:=(\|a\|_\infty+\|\nabla a\|_\infty)\1_{\operatorname{supp} a}$, which is bounded with compact support in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Since $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}$ is constant by Proposition \ref{propcompact} (ii), Lemma \ref{lemmaweak} gives $S(-t)u(t)\rightharpoonup\mathcal{B} a$ as $t\to\pm\infty$. The same holds for the coefficient $sa$, $s\in\mathbb{R}$: $S(-t)u_s(t)\rightharpoonup s\mathcal{B} a$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Small amplitudes. We use the results of \cite{HHK,HHKcorr}, transferred to \eqref{kp} by the change of variables of Subsection \ref{subsectionkp}, which preserves the spaces $\dot H^{-\frac12,0}$ and $L^2$ up to constant factors and intertwines the translations and the free groups. By \cite[Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.7]{HHK}, there is $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that every initial datum $U_0$ with $\|U_0\|_{\dot H^{-\frac12,0}}<\varepsilon_0$ generates a global solution $U\in C([0,\infty);\dot H^{-\frac12,0})$, unique in the function space of \cite[Theorem 1.1]{HHK}, the map $U_0\mapsto U$ is analytic into $C([0,\infty);\dot H^{-\frac12,0})$, and there is a state $U_+$ with $\|U(t)-S(t)U_+\|_{\dot H^{-\frac12,0}}\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$; if moreover $U_0\in L^2$ is real, then $\|U_+\|_{L^2}=\|U_0\|_{L^2}$. By \eqref{smallcritical}, there is $s_*>0$ such that $U_0:=u_s(0)$ is admissible for $|s|\le s_*$. Let $U$ be the corresponding solution. Since $u_s(0)$ is real, $\overline U$ solves the same equation with the same datum, and $U$ is real by uniqueness.

{\it Regularity of $U$.} By uniqueness and translation invariance of the equation, the flow map commutes with translations: the solution with datum $\tau_hU_0$ is $\tau_hU$. By \eqref{smallcritical}, $h\mapsto\tau_hU_0$ is a $C^\infty$ map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ into $\dot H^{-\frac12,0}$. Composing with the analytic flow map, $h\mapsto\tau_hU$ is $C^\infty$ into $C([0,\infty);\dot H^{-\frac12,0})$, and its derivatives at $h=0$ are the distributional derivatives of $U$. Hence $\partial^\gamma_XU\in C([0,\infty);\dot H^{-\frac12,0})$ for every $\gamma$. Since $1\le|\xi|^{-1}+|\xi|$,
$$\|f\|_{L^2}^2\le\|f\|_{\dot H^{-\frac12,0}}^2+\|\partial_xf\|_{\dot H^{-\frac12,0}}^2,$$
so that $\partial^\gamma_XU\in C([0,\infty);L^2)$ for every $\gamma$, and in particular $U$ and $\partial_xU$ are bounded on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^2$ for every $T>0$, by Sobolev embedding.

{\it Uniqueness.} The solution $U$ satisfies the Duhamel formula \cite[Remark 1.3]{HHK}, in which the Duhamel term coincides with the Bochner integral of \eqref{duhamel}, since $U\partial_xU\in L^\infty([0,T];L^2)$; the smooth solution $u_s$ satisfies \eqref{duhamel} by Proposition \ref{propcompact} (ii). Both are real and bounded with bounded $x$-derivatives on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^2$ for every $T>0$, by the regularity of $U$ and by Proposition \ref{propcompact} (i), so that Lemma \ref{lemmaunique} gives $U=u_s$ on $[0,\infty)$.

{\it Identification of the state.} Let $\hat\varphi\in C^\infty_c(\{\xi\neq0\})$; then $\varphi$ belongs to the space $\dot H^{\frac12,0}$, defined by the norm $\||\xi|^{\frac12}\hat\varphi\|_{L^2}$, which is the dual space of $\dot H^{-\frac12,0}$ for the pairing $(\cdot,\cdot)$. By Step 1 and by the convergence in $\dot H^{-\frac12,0}$, $(S(-t)u_s(t),\varphi)$ converges both to $(s\mathcal{B} a,\varphi)$ and to $(U_+,\varphi)$. Hence $\widehat{U_+}=s\widehat{\mathcal{B} a}$ almost everywhere, and
$$\|u_s(0)\|_{L^2}^2=\|U_+\|_{L^2}^2=s^2\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\mbox{for}\ |s|\le s_* .$$

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Analytic continuation. By Proposition \ref{propcompact} (iv), $s\mapsto\|u_s(0)\|_{L^2}^2$ is real-analytic on $\mathbb{R}$. It coincides with $s^2\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}^2$ on $[-s_*,s_*]$, hence on $\mathbb{R}$. For $s=1$ and with \eqref{bornisometry}, this is \eqref{plancherelcompact}.

We bound the operator norm by $\sup_X\int|G_k(X-X')||f(X')|dX'$. If $|k_1|\ge2$, we split according to $|y-y'|<|k_1|^{-2}$ or not. The first part is at most $\|f\|_{L^\infty}\int_{|x'|\le L}\int_{|y-y'|<|k_1|^{-2}}|y-y'|^{-\frac12}dy'dx'\lesssim L\|f\|_{L^\infty}|k_1|^{-1}$. In the second part we use the bound $(|x-x'+2k_1(y-y')|+|k_1|^{-1})^{-1}$; for fixed $x'$, the substitution $y'\mapsto z:=x-x'+2k_1(y-y')$ maps $[-L,L]$ onto an interval of length $4|k_1|L$, and $\int_I\frac{dz}{|z|+\varepsilon}\le2\log\big(1+\frac{|I|}{2\varepsilon}\big)$ for an interval $I$, so that this part is at most
$$\|f\|_{L^\infty}\int_{|x'|\le L}\frac1{2|k_1|}\,2\log\big(1+2k_1^2L\big)\,dx'\lesssim L\|f\|_{L^\infty}\frac{\log(2+k_1^2L)}{|k_1|}.$$
If $|k_2|\ge2$, we use the bound $\min(|y|^{-\frac12},(|k_2||y|)^{-1})$ of \eqref{sizegreen} and split at $|y-y'|=|k_2|^{-2}$ and $|y-y'|=1$: this gives the bound $C\big(\|f\|_{L^1}+\sup_{y}\|f(\cdot,y)\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}\big)\frac{1+\log|k_2|}{|k_2|}$. Both bounds tend to zero as $|k|\to\infty$. For $f\in\mathcal{K}_0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $f_\varepsilon\in C^\infty_c$ with $\|f-f_\varepsilon\|_\mathcal{K}\le\varepsilon$; by (i), $\|G_k\ast(f\,\cdot)\|\le C\varepsilon+\|G_k\ast(f_\varepsilon\,\cdot)\|$. The same $f_\varepsilon$ works, with $2\varepsilon$, for all the terms of a sequence converging to $f$ in $\mathcal{K}$, except finitely many.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} The real axis. Let $k=k_1\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $C_1\ge1$ be the constant in (i). Choose $f\in C^\infty_c$, supported in $[-L,L]^2$, with $\|u_0-f\|_\mathcal{K}\le(16C_1)^{-1}$. For an interval $I$, \eqref{defK} gives $\|f\1_{\{y\in I\}}\|_\mathcal{K}\le\|f\|_{L^\infty}\cdot2L\cdot2\sqrt{2|I|}$. Hence we can partition $\mathbb{R}$ into ordered intervals $I_1<I_2<\dots<I_J$, with $I_1$ and $I_J$ unbounded and $J$ depending only on $u_0$, such that $C_1\|f\1_{\{y\in I_j\}}\|_\mathcal{K}\le\frac18$ for every $j$. Let $\tilde u_0\in\mathcal{K}$ with $\|\tilde u_0-u_0\|_\mathcal{K}\le(16C_1)^{-1}$; for instance $\tilde u_0=u_0$, or $\tilde u_0=u_{0,n}$ with $n$ large. The functions $\tilde u_j:=\tilde u_0\1_{\{y\in I_j\}}$ satisfy $C_1\|\tilde u_j\|_\mathcal{K}\le\frac18+\frac1{16}+\frac1{16}=\frac14$. Since $G_{k_1}(x,y)=0$ for $y<0$, the value of $G_{k_1}\ast(\tilde u_0H)$ on the strip $\{y\in I_j\}$ depends only on the restrictions $H_l:=H\1_{\{y\in I_l\}}$, $l\le j$. The equation $H-G_{k_1}\ast(\tilde u_0H)=b$ is therefore equivalent to the triangular system
$$H_j-\1_{\{y\in I_j\}}G_{k_1}\ast(\tilde u_jH_j)=\1_{\{y\in I_j\}}\Big(b+\sum_{l<j}G_{k_1}\ast(\tilde u_lH_l)\Big),\qquad j=1,\dots,J,$$
whose diagonal operators have norm at most $\frac14$. Solving successively by Neumann series, the operator $H\mapsto H-G_{k_1}\ast(\tilde u_0H)$ is invertible, with inverse bounded by a constant $C_J$ which depends only on $J$, and not on $k_1$ or on $\tilde u_0$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Proof of (iii). If $u_0=0$, then $T_k=I$ for every $k$. Moreover, by (i) and $\|u_{0,n}\|_\mathcal{K}\to0$, we have $\sup_{k\in\mathbb{C}}\|G_k\ast(u_{0,n}\,\cdot\,)\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}\le\frac12$ for $n$ large, so a Neumann series gives the assertion with $R_0=1$. We may therefore assume $u_0\neq0$. By (i), $\|T_k-T_{k_1}\|\le C|k_2|\|u_0\|_{L^1}$ for $k=k_1+ik_2$, so that a Neumann series gives the invertibility of $T_k$ with $\|T_k^{-1}\|\le2C_J$ for $|k_2|\le(4CC_J\|u_0\|_{L^1})^{-1}$; the same holds for $u_{0,n}$ when $|k_2|\le(8CC_J\|u_0\|_{L^1})^{-1}$ and $\|u_{0,n}\|_{L^1}\le2\|u_0\|_{L^1}$. By (ii), $\|G_k\ast(u_0\,\cdot)\|\le\frac12$, hence $\|T_k^{-1}\|\le2$, for $|k|\ge R$, with $R$ large, and by Step 1 the same $R$ works for $u_{0,n}$, $n$ large. We choose $R_0\ge\max(1,R,8CC_J\|u_0\|_{L^1})$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Proof of (iv). Let $\tilde H_j:=T_k^{-1}H_j$ and $\Phi_j:=G_k\ast(u_0\tilde H_j)=\tilde H_j-H_j$. The $\Phi_j$ are uniformly bounded, and they are uniformly equicontinuous:
$$|\Phi_j(X+h)-\Phi_j(X)|\le\sup_l\|\tilde H_l\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}|G_k(Z+h)-G_k(Z)|\,|u_0(X-Z)|\,dZ ,$$
and the right-hand side tends to zero as $h\to0$ uniformly in $X$: on $\{|Z|\le r\}$ we use $\|u_0\|_{L^\infty}$ and the local integrability of $G_k$ given by \eqref{sizegreen}, and on $\{|Z|\ge r\}$ we use $\|u_0\|_{L^1}$ and the uniform continuity of $G_k$ there, which follows from Lemma \ref{lemmagreen} (i) and \eqref{sizegreen}. By the Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem, every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $\Phi_j\to\Phi$ locally uniformly, so that $\tilde H_j\to\tilde H:=H+\Phi$ pointwise and boundedly. By dominated convergence, $\Phi=G_k\ast(u_0\tilde H)$, that is, $T_k\tilde H=H$ and $\tilde H=T_k^{-1}H$. Since the limit does not depend on the subsequence, $\tilde H_j\to T_k^{-1}H$ pointwise.

name: Irregular points

title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Reduction to a Hilbert--Schmidt operator. For $c\in\mathbb{R}$ let $g_c(x,y):=(|x+2cy|+|y|^{\frac12})^{-1}$, so that $|G_k|\lesssim g_{k_1}$ by \eqref{sizegreen}. The function $g_c$ is square integrable on the unit disc $D(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, with
$$\int_{D(0,1)}g_c^2\,dX\le\int_{-1}^1\int_\mathbb{R}\frac{ds}{(|s|+|y|^{\frac12})^2}\,dy=\int_{-1}^1\frac{2\,dy}{|y|^{\frac12}}=8,$$
and $g_c\le4\langle c\rangle$ outside $D(0,1)$: if $|y|\ge(16\langle c\rangle^2)^{-1}$, then $g_c\le|y|^{-\frac12}$, and otherwise $|x|\ge\frac12$ and $|x+2cy|\ge\frac12-\frac18$. We write $u_0=|u_0|^{\frac12}u_0^{\frac12}$, with $u_0^{\frac12}:=\operatorname{sgn}(u_0)|u_0|^{\frac12}$; both factors belong to $L^2\cap L^\infty$ by \eqref{expdecay}. For $k\in\mathbb{C}$ let $Q_k$ be the operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ with kernel $|u_0(X)|^{\frac12}G_k(X-X')u_0^{\frac12}(X')$. Splitting $G_k=G_k\1_{D(0,1)}+G_k\1_{\mathbb{R}^2\setminus D(0,1)}$, we see that $Q_k$ is a Hilbert--Schmidt operator,
$$\begin{aligned}\|Q_k\|_{\rm HS}^2&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}|u_0(X)||G_k(X-X')|^2|u_0(X')|\,dX\,dX'\\&\lesssim\|u_0\|_{L^\infty}\|u_0\|_{L^1}+\langle k\rangle^2\|u_0\|_{L^1}^2,\end{aligned}$$
and that $G_k\ast(u_0^{\frac12}\varphi)\in L^\infty$ for $\varphi\in L^2$, since $u_0^{\frac12}\varphi\in L^1\cap L^2$. If $H\in L^\infty$ and $T_kH=0$, then $\varphi:=|u_0|^{\frac12}H\in L^2$ satisfies $Q_k\varphi=|u_0|^{\frac12}G_k\ast(u_0H)=\varphi$. Conversely, if $\varphi\in L^2$ and $Q_k\varphi=\varphi$, then $H:=G_k\ast(u_0^{\frac12}\varphi)\in L^\infty$ satisfies $|u_0|^{\frac12}H=\varphi$, hence $u_0H=u_0^{\frac12}\varphi$ and $T_kH=0$. Since $|u_0|^{\frac12}H=0$ implies $u_0H=0$ and then $H=G_k\ast(u_0H)=0$, the map $H\mapsto|u_0|^{\frac12}H$ is a bijection from the kernel of $T_k$ onto the kernel of $I-Q_k$. If the latter is trivial, then $I-Q_k$ is invertible by the Fredholm alternative, and a direct computation shows that
$$T_k^{-1}b=b+G_k\ast\big(u_0^{\frac12}(I-Q_k)^{-1}(|u_0|^{\frac12}b)\big),\qquad b\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2).$$
Therefore $k$ is a regular point if and only if $I-Q_k$ is invertible, that is, if and only if $\Xi(k):=\det_2(I-Q_k)\neq0$, where $\det_2$ is the regularized Fredholm determinant on the Hilbert--Schmidt class \cite[Chapter 9]{Simon}.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} $\Sigma$ is closed. By Lemma \ref{lemmagreenop} (i), $\|T_k-T_{k'}\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}\lesssim|k-k'|\|u_0\|_{L^1}$. Since the set of invertible operators is open, the set of regular points is open, and $\|T_k^{-1}\|$ is locally bounded on it. By Lemma \ref{lemmagreenop} (iii), $\Sigma\subset\{|k|\le R_0,\ |k_2|\ge R_0^{-1}\}$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Analyticity of $\Xi$. Let $k_2>0$. Substituting $s=\pm(k_2+r)$, $r>0$, if $y>0$, and $s=k_2\sigma$, $|\sigma|<1$, if $y<0$, in \eqref{formulagreen}, we obtain, with $\tilde x=x+2k_1y$,
$$G_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\big(e^{ir\tilde x}+e^{-i(2k_2+r)\tilde x}\big)e^{-(r^2+2k_2r)y}\,dr,& y>0,\\[3mm] \displaystyle-\frac{k_2}{2\pi}\int_{-1}^1e^{-ik_2(1-\sigma)\tilde x-k_2^2(1-\sigma^2)|y|}\,d\sigma,& y<0.\end{cases}$$
For fixed $X$ with $y\neq0$, the right-hand sides are entire functions of $(k_1,k_2)\in\mathbb{C}^2$, which we denote by $\tilde G(k_1,k_2;X)$. Fix $k^0=(k^0_1,k^0_2)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty)$ and let $(k_1,k_2)=(p_1+iq_1,p_2+iq_2)\in\mathbb{C}^2$ with $|k_j-k^0_j|\le2\mu$, $j=1,2$, where $0<\mu\le\frac{k^0_2}8$ is chosen below. Then $p_2\pm q_1\ge0$ and $p_2^2-q_2^2\ge0$. For $y>0$, the first integrand is $e^{ir(x+2(p_1-q_2)y)}$ times the weight $e^{-r^2y-2(p_2+q_1)ry}$, which decreases from $1$ to $0$, and the second one is $e^{-2ik_2\tilde x}e^{-ir(x+2(p_1+q_2)y)}$ times the decreasing weight $e^{-r^2y-2(p_2-q_1)ry}$. The integration by parts of Step 2 of the proof of Lemma \ref{lemmagreen}, together with $\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2y}dr\lesssim y^{-\frac12}$, and the bound $|e^{-k_2^2(1-\sigma^2)|y|}|\le1$ for $y<0$, give
$$|\tilde G(k_1,k_2;X)|\lesssim e^{2|\operatorname{Im}(k_2\tilde x)|}\big(\langle k^0\rangle+g_{p_1-q_2}(X)+g_{p_1+q_2}(X)\big),$$
where $|\operatorname{Im}(k_2\tilde x)|=|q_2x+2(p_1q_2+q_1p_2)y|\le C\mu\langle k^0\rangle|X|$. We choose $\mu$ so small that $4C\mu\langle k^0\rangle\le\frac\varepsilon2$. Since $e^{-\varepsilon(|X|+|X'|)}e^{\frac\varepsilon2|X-X'|}\le e^{-\frac\varepsilon2(|X|+|X'|)}$, Step 1 shows that the operators $\tilde Q(k_1,k_2)$ with kernels $|u_0(X)|^{\frac12}\tilde G(k_1,k_2;X-X')u_0^{\frac12}(X')$ satisfy $\|\tilde Q(k_1,k_2)\|_{\rm HS}\lesssim_{k^0}1$ for $|k_j-k^0_j|\le2\mu$. By the Cauchy formula on the torus $\{|z_j-k^0_j|=2\mu\}$ and Minkowski's inequality, the operators $Q^{(\gamma)}$, $\gamma\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}^2$, whose kernels are given by the Taylor coefficients of $\tilde G$ at $k^0$, satisfy $\|Q^{(\gamma)}\|_{\rm HS}\lesssim_{k^0}(2\mu)^{-|\gamma|}$. Hence the series $\sum_\gamma(k_1-k^0_1)^{\gamma_1}(k_2-k^0_2)^{\gamma_2}Q^{(\gamma)}$ converges in the Hilbert--Schmidt norm for $|k_j-k^0_j|<\mu$, and its sum is $\tilde Q(k_1,k_2)$, since the Taylor series of $\tilde G$ converges pointwise. Thus $(k_1,k_2)\mapsto\tilde Q(k_1,k_2)$ is holomorphic with values in the Hilbert--Schmidt class, and since $A\mapsto\det_2(I-A)$ is holomorphic on this class \cite[Chapter 9]{Simon}, $\det_2(I-\tilde Q)$ is a holomorphic extension of $\Xi$ near $k^0_1+ik^0_2$. Hence $\Xi$ is real-analytic on $\mathbb{C}^+$. By Lemma \ref{lemmagreen} (iv), $Q_{\bar k}$ is the complex conjugate of $Q_k$, so that $\Xi(\bar k)=\overline{\Xi(k)}$, and $\Xi$ is real-analytic on $\mathbb{C}^-$ as well.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Conclusion. By Step 1 and Lemma \ref{lemmagreenop} (iii), $\Xi(k)\neq0$ for $|k|>R_0$. If $\Sigma$ contained a nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}^\pm$, then $\Xi$ would vanish on $U$, hence on the connected open set $\mathbb{C}^\pm$ by real-analyticity, a contradiction. Hence $\Sigma$ has empty interior.

$$\big\|\varrho_{\varepsilon_n}\ast\big(\vartheta(\cdot/n)u_0\big)-\vartheta(\cdot/n)u_0\big\|_{L^1\cap L^2}+\big\|\varrho_{\varepsilon_n}\ast\big(\vartheta(\cdot/n)f\big)-\vartheta(\cdot/n)f\big\|_{L^1}\le\frac1n .$$

Moreover $|\nabla\langle X\rangle^\theta|\le\theta$ and $\langle X-Z\rangle\ge1$ give $|\mu_Z-1|\le\theta|Z|$. Hence \eqref{weightconv} gives
$$\big\|\langle X\rangle^\theta u_{0,n}-\varrho_{\varepsilon_n}\ast\big(\vartheta(\cdot/n)f\big)\big\|_{L^1}\le\theta\varepsilon_n\|f\|_{L^1},$$
and, by the choice of $\varepsilon_n$, $\langle X\rangle^\theta u_{0,n}\to f$ in $L^1$. A convergent sequence in $L^1$ is bounded and tight, which gives \eqref{tightmoment}.

{\bf Step 1:} Proof of (i). Let $g:=\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf$. Let $\kappa$ be the Schwartz function on $\mathbb{R}$ of the proof of Lemma \ref{lemmaembedding}, with $\kappa\ast g=g$ whenever $\hat g$ is supported in $[-2,2]$, and $\kappa_j:=2^j\kappa(2^j\cdot)$. Since $\hat g$ is supported in $\{|\xi|\le2^{j+1}\}$, we have $g=\kappa_j\ast_xg$, hence $\partial_xg=\kappa_j'\ast_xg$ with $\|\kappa_j'\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}=2^j\|\kappa'\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}$. By Minkowski's inequality and the invariance of $\|\cdot\|_Y$ under translations, $\|\partial_xg\|_Y\lesssim2^j\|g\|_Y$, and since $\|\delta^x_hg\|_Y\le\min(2\|g\|_Y,|h|\|\partial_xg\|_Y)$,
$$\|\delta^x_hg\|_Y\lesssim\min(1,2^j|h|)\|g\|_Y,\qquad \|\delta^y_{h'}g\|_Y\lesssim\min(1,2^l|h'|)\|g\|_Y,$$
where the second bound is obtained in the same way. Applying the first bound to $\delta^y_{h'}g$, whose Fourier transform is supported in that of $g$, we also obtain $\|\delta^x_h\delta^y_{h'}g\|_Y\lesssim\min(1,2^j|h|)\min(1,2^l|h'|)\|g\|_Y$. The series $f=\sum_{j,l}\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf$ converges absolutely in $Y$. Let $\alpha\le1$. Summing over $(j,l)$ and using $\min(1,2^j|h|)\le(2^j|h|)^\alpha$ and $\min(1,2^l|h'|)\le(2^l|h'|)^\beta$, we obtain, for instance, $\|\delta^x_h\delta^y_{h'}f\|_Y\lesssim|h|^\alpha|h'|^\beta N_{\alpha,\beta}(f;Y)$, and the other terms of \eqref{defmixed} are bounded in the same way. If $1<\alpha<2$, the bound $\|\partial_x\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf\|_Y\lesssim2^j\|\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf\|_Y$ gives $N_{1,\beta}(f;Y)+N_{\alpha-1,\beta}(\partial_xf;Y)\lesssim N_{\alpha,\beta}(f;Y)$, and the case $\alpha\le1$ applies to $f$ and to $\partial_xf$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Proof of (ii). Let $\alpha\le1$. By \eqref{productrule} with $h=(h_1,0)$ and $h'=(0,h_2)$,
$$\begin{aligned}\delta^x_{h_1}\delta^y_{h_2}(fg)&=(\delta^x_{h_1}\delta^y_{h_2}f)\,\tau_{(h_1,h_2)}g+(\delta^x_{h_1}f)\,\tau_{(h_1,0)}\delta^y_{h_2}g\\&\quad+(\delta^y_{h_2}f)\,\tau_{(0,h_2)}\delta^x_{h_1}g+f\,\delta^x_{h_1}\delta^y_{h_2}g,\end{aligned}$$
and the bound $\|cf\|_Y\le\|c\|_{L^\infty}\|f\|_Y$, which holds by \eqref{propK} for $Y=\mathcal{K}$, shows that each term has norm at most $|h_1|^\alpha|h_2|^\beta\|f\|_{\alpha,\beta;Y}\|g\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}$. The other terms of \eqref{defmixed} are treated in the same way. If $1<\alpha<2$, we apply the case $\alpha\le1$ to $fg$, with the exponent $1$, and to $\partial_x(fg)=(\partial_xf)g+f\partial_xg$, with the exponent $\alpha-1$, and we use $\|\cdot\|_{\alpha-1,\beta;Y}\le3\|\cdot\|_{1,\beta;Y}$. Finally, $\|\delta^x_hc\|_{L^\infty}\le2\min(1,|h|)\|c\|_{W^{1,\infty}}$, and $\|\delta^x_h\delta^y_{h'}c\|_{L^\infty}$ is bounded by each of $4\|c\|_{L^\infty}$, $2|h|\|\partial_xc\|_{L^\infty}$, $2|h'|\|\partial_yc\|_{L^\infty}$ and $|h||h'|\|\partial_x\partial_yc\|_{L^\infty}$, hence by $4\min(1,|h|)\min(1,|h'|)\|c\|_{W^{2,\infty}}$. This gives $\|c\|_{1,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim\|c\|_{W^{2,\infty}}$, and the bound on $\|c\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}$ follows, applied to $c$ and to $\partial_xc$ if $\alpha>1$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Proof of (iii). Let $\alpha\le1$. Since $\widehat{\delta^x_h\delta^y_{h'}\Phi}(\xi,\eta)=(e^{ih\xi}-1)(e^{ih'\eta}-1)\hat\Phi(\xi,\eta)$, the choice $h=\pi/\xi$, $h'=\pi/\eta$ gives, when $|\xi|,|\eta|\ge1$,
$$4|\hat\Phi(\xi,\eta)|\le\frac1{2\pi}\|\delta^x_h\delta^y_{h'}\Phi\|_{L^1}\le\frac1{2\pi}\Big(\frac\pi{|\xi|}\Big)^\alpha\Big(\frac\pi{|\eta|}\Big)^\beta\|\Phi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^1}.$$
Omitting one or both differences when $|\xi|<1$ or $|\eta|<1$ gives (iii). If $1<\alpha<2$, we apply this to $\Phi$ with the exponent $1$ and to $\partial_x\Phi$ with the exponent $\alpha-1$, and we use $|\hat\Phi|=|\xi|^{-1}|\widehat{\partial_x\Phi}|$ for $|\xi|\ge1$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Proof of (iv). We write $u:=u_0$, $\chi:=\chi_k$, and we apply Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (i), (ii) with $h=(h_1,0)$ and $h'=(0,h_2)$, to the equations of Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (iii), so that $\delta_h=\delta^x_{h_1}$ and $\delta_{h'}=\delta^y_{h_2}$. Let first $\alpha\le1$. With $g=\chi-1$ and $(f_1,f_2)=(u,0)$, and since $\|\chi\|_{L^\infty}\le\Lambda$, Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (i) gives $\|\delta^x_{h_1}\chi\|_{L^\infty}\lesssim|h_1|^\alpha$ and $\|\delta^y_{h_2}\chi\|_{L^\infty}\lesssim|h_2|^\beta$, and then Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (ii) gives $\|\delta^y_{h_2}\delta^x_{h_1}\chi\|_{L^\infty}\lesssim|h_1|^\alpha|h_2|^\beta$. Hence $\|\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$, and $\|u\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^1}\lesssim1$ by (ii). With $g=\partial_e\chi$, which is bounded by \eqref{dkchi}, and $(f_1,f_2)=(0,u\chi)$, the same argument gives $\|\partial_e\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$.

Let now $1<\alpha<2$. By \eqref{derivativeschi}, $\|\partial_x\chi\|_{L^\infty}\le C\Lambda\|\partial_xu\|_\mathcal{K}\|\chi\|_{L^\infty}\lesssim1$. Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (i), with $(0,h_2)$ in place of $h$, applied to $g=\chi-1$ and to $g=\partial_x\chi$, whose data are $(f_1,f_2)=((\partial_xu)\chi,0)$, gives $\|\delta^y_{h_2}\chi\|_{L^\infty}+\|\delta^y_{h_2}\partial_x\chi\|_{L^\infty}\lesssim|h_2|^\beta$, where we used $\delta^y_{h_2}((\partial_xu)\chi)=(\delta^y_{h_2}\partial_xu)\,\tau_{(0,h_2)}\chi+(\partial_xu)\,\delta^y_{h_2}\chi$. By \eqref{mixedone}, $\|\chi\|_{1,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$. Since $\|u\|_{\alpha-1,\beta;\mathcal{K}}\le3\|u\|_{\alpha,\beta;\mathcal{K}}$ and $\|(\partial_xu)\chi\|_{\alpha-1,\beta;\mathcal{K}}\lesssim\|\partial_xu\|_{\alpha-1,\beta;\mathcal{K}}\|\chi\|_{1,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$ by (ii), the argument of the case $\alpha\le1$, with the exponent $\alpha-1$ and applied to $g=\partial_x\chi$, gives $\|\partial_x\chi\|_{\alpha-1,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$. Hence $\|\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$, and $\|u\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^1}\lesssim1$ by (ii). The same argument, with $g=\partial_e\chi$ and $g=\partial_x\partial_e\chi$, whose data $(0,u\chi)$ and $((\partial_xu)\partial_e\chi,\partial_x(u\chi))$ are given in Lemma \ref{lemmadifferences} (iii), gives $\|\partial_e\chi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^\infty}\lesssim1$.

body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Bounds on $\Omega$. By (i) and Lemma \ref{lemmaembedding} (i), $u_0\in\mathcal{K}_0\cap L^1$ and $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $\mathcal{K}\cap L^1$. By Lemma \ref{lemmagreenop} (iii), there are $R_0$, $\Lambda$ and $n_0$ such that, for $n\ge n_0$, the operators $T_k$ of $u_{0,n}$ satisfy $\|T_k^{-1}\|\le\Lambda$ on $\Omega=\{|k|>R_0\}\cup\{|k_2|<R_0^{-1}\}$. The finitely many $a_n$ with $n<n_0$ satisfy \eqref{envelopemixed} by \eqref{hypa}, since $\langle \zeta\rangle^{-4}\le F_{\alpha,\beta}$. Let $n\ge n_0$ and $k\in\Omega\setminus\mathbb{R}$, and write $u:=u_{0,n}$ and $\chi:=\chi_n(k;\cdot)$, where $\chi_n$ is the eigenfunction \eqref{defchi} of $u_{0,n}$. By Lemma \ref{lemmamixednorm} (iv) and (ii), and by (iii), the functions
$$\Phi\in\big\{u\chi,\ u\,\partial_e\chi,\ xu\chi,\ yu\chi\big\},\qquad e\in\{1,i\},$$
satisfy $\|\Phi\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^1}\lesssim1$, uniformly in $n$ and $k$. By Lemma \ref{lemmamixednorm} (iii), $|\hat\Phi(\zeta(k))|\lesssim F_{\alpha,\beta}(k)$. With $\Phi=u\chi$, \eqref{defa} gives $|a_n(k)|\lesssim F_{\alpha,\beta}(k)$. The formula \eqref{dka} expresses $\partial_ea_n(k)$ through $\hat\Phi(\zeta(k))$ for $\Phi\in\{u\,\partial_e\chi,\ xu\chi,\ yu\chi\}$, with coefficients bounded by $|\partial_e\zeta(k)|\le4\langle k\rangle$, which gives $|\nabla_ka_n(k)|\lesssim\langle k\rangle F_{\alpha,\beta}(k)$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Bounds on the compact set $K:=\{|k|\le R_0,\ |k_2|\ge R_0^{-1}\}$. By Step 1, $|a_n|\lesssim F_{\alpha,\beta}$ outside $K$, and $\mathcal{I} F_{\alpha,\beta}$ is bounded by Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (i). By (i) and (ii), Lemma \ref{lemmabootstrap} applies with $\theta=1$: its parts (i) and (iii) give $\sup_n\sup_{K'}(|a_n|+|\nabla_ka_n|)<\infty$ for every compact set $K'\subset\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Since $F_{\alpha,\beta}$ is bounded below on $K$, \eqref{envelopemixed} holds on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Finally, every compact subset of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$ is covered by finitely many discs contained in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, on which the $a_n$ are uniformly bounded and uniformly Lipschitz, and the Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem, with a diagonal argument, gives the convergent subsequence.

label: upperbound
title: Proof
body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Upper bound. By Corollary \ref{corsmooth}, $\|\mathcal{B} a_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_{0,n}\|_{L^2}\to\|u_0\|_{L^2}$. Since $a_n\to a$ pointwise on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, Fatou's lemma gives
\begin{equation}
\label{upperbound}
\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}^2=8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2||a|^2\,dA\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2||a_n|^2\,dA=\|u_0\|_{L^2}^2 ;
\end{equation}
in particular $\mathcal{B} a\in L^2$. If $\hat\varphi\in C^\infty_c(\{\xi\neq0\})$, then, by the Plancherel identity, \eqref{defborn} and \eqref{changevariables},
$$\big(\mathcal{B} a_n,\varphi\big)=8\int_\mathbb{C} i\operatorname{sgn}(k_2)\,a_n(k)\,\overline{\hat\varphi(\zeta(k))}\,|k_2|\,dA(k)$$
is an integral over a fixed compact subset of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, which converges to $(\mathcal{B} a,\varphi)$. Since these functions $\varphi$ are dense in $L^2$ and $(\mathcal{B} a_n)$ is bounded in $L^2$, $\mathcal{B} a_n\rightharpoonup\mathcal{B} a$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} The eigenfunctions. The limit $a$ is continuous on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, real, and satisfies $|a|\le F$, so that $\mathcal{I}|a|\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$ by Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (iv). Let $m_n$ and $m$ be the eigenfunctions \eqref{eqm} of $a_n$ and $a$ at $t=0$, given by Lemma \ref{lemmavekua} (ii), and $M:=\|\mathcal{I} F\|_\infty$. By Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (v), applied with the majorant $2F$, $\|\mathcal{I}|a_n-a|\|_\infty\to0$, and by \eqref{comparison}, $\sup_{k,X}|m_n(k;0,X)-m(k;0,X)|\to0$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Compactly supported approximation of $a$. Let $\vartheta_R$ be the cutoff of Step 1 of the proof of Proposition \ref{proprapid}, $b_R:=\vartheta_Ra$ and $\tilde a_R:=\varrho_\varepsilon\ast b_R$, where $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_R\le(8R)^{-1}$ will be chosen small. Then $\tilde a_R\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R})$ is real, since $\varrho$ is radial. By Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (iv) and (v), $\|\mathcal{I}|b_R-a|\|_\infty\le\|\mathcal{I}\big(F\1_{\{|k|>R\}\cup\{|k_2|<R^{-1}\}}\big)\|_\infty\to0$, and by \eqref{upperbound} and dominated convergence, $\int|k_2||b_R-a|^2dA\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. The function $g:=|\tilde a_R-b_R|$ is bounded by $2\|F\|_\infty$, supported in $\{|k|\le3R\}$, and tends to zero in $L^1(\mathbb{C})$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. By the last bound of \eqref{potentialsets}, $\|\mathcal{I} g\|_\infty\le2(\|g\|_\infty\|g\|_{L^1})^{\frac12}$, and $\int|k_2|g^2\,dA\le3R\|g\|_\infty\|g\|_{L^1}$. Hence we can choose $\varepsilon_R$ such that
$$\|\mathcal{I}|\tilde a_R-a|\|_\infty\to0,\qquad 8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2||\tilde a_R-a|^2\,dA\to0\qquad(R\to\infty).$$
Let $\tilde m_R$ and $\tilde u_R$ be the eigenfunction and the function reconstructed from $\tilde a_R$ at $t=0$. By \eqref{comparison}, $\tilde m_R\to m$ uniformly in $(k,X)$, and by Proposition \ref{propplancherel},
$$\|\tilde u_R\|_{L^2}^2=8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2||\tilde a_R|^2\,dA\longrightarrow8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2||a|^2\,dA=\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}^2 .$$
Up to a subsequence, $\tilde u_R\rightharpoonup u_*$ in $L^2$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} The heat equation. Since $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $L^1\cap L^2$, Lemma \ref{lemmaembedding} (i) gives $u_0\in\mathcal{K}_0\cap L^1$ and $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $\mathcal{K}\cap L^1$, and by Lemma \ref{lemmagreenop} (iii) there is $R_0$ such that every $k$ with $|k|>R_0$ is a regular point of $u_{0,n}$ for $n$ large. Since $\mathcal{I} F\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$, we can fix $k\notin\mathbb{R}$ with $|k|>R_0$ and $e^{2M}\mathcal{I} F(k)<\frac12$. By Proposition \ref{propcompact} (iii), $\partial_y\tilde m_R-\partial_x^2\tilde m_R-2k\partial_x\tilde m_R-\tilde u_R\tilde m_R=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Since $\tilde m_R\to m$ uniformly and $\tilde u_R\rightharpoonup u_*$ in $L^2$, we have $\tilde u_R\tilde m_R\to u_*m$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb{R}^2)$, and therefore
$$\partial_ym-\partial_x^2m-2k\partial_xm-u_*m=0\qquad\mbox{in}\ \mathcal D'(\mathbb{R}^2).$$
By Proposition \ref{propdirect} (ii) and \eqref{eqchi}, $\partial_ym_n-\partial_x^2m_n-2k\partial_xm_n-u_{0,n}m_n=0$, and Step 2 together with $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $L^2$ gives the same equation with $u_0$ in place of $u_*$. Subtracting, $(u_*-u_0)\,m(k;0,\cdot)=0$. By \eqref{boundeigen}, $|m(k;0,X)-1|\le e^{2M}\mathcal{I} F(k)<\frac12$ for every $X$, hence $u_*=u_0$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 5:} Conclusion. By weak lower semicontinuity, $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|u_*\|_{L^2}\le\liminf_R\|\tilde u_R\|_{L^2}=\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}$. Together with \eqref{upperbound}, $\|\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\lim_n\|\mathcal{B} a_n\|_{L^2}$, and the weak convergence $\mathcal{B} a_n\rightharpoonup\mathcal{B} a$ becomes strong.

body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Choice of the exponents. Choose $0<s_1'<\min(s_1,3)$ and $0<s_2'<\min(s_2,2)$ with $s':=s_1'+2s_2'>3$. The open intervals
$$I_1:=\big(\max(0,s_1'-2),\,\min(1,s_1')\big),\qquad I_2:=\big(\max(0,s_2'-1),\,\min(1,s_2')\big)$$
are nonempty, and $I_1+2I_2$ is an open interval. Its supremum $\min(1,s_1')+2\min(1,s_2')$ is larger than $1$: since $s'>3$, we have $s_1'\ge1$ or $s_2'\ge1$; in the first case the supremum is $1+2\min(1,s_2')$, and in the second one it is $\min(1,s_1')+2$. Its infimum $\max(0,s_1'-2)+2\max(0,s_2'-1)$ is smaller than $s'-2$: according to whether $s_1'>2$ and whether $s_2'>1$, the difference between $s'-2$ and the infimum equals $s'-2$, $2s_2'$, $s_1'$ or $2$, which are all positive. Since also $s'-2>1$, we can choose $d_1\in I_1$ and $d_2\in I_2$ with $1<d_1+2d_2<s'-2$. Let
$$p:=(1-d_1)^{-1},\qquad q:=(1-d_2)^{-1},\qquad \alpha:=s_1'-d_1,\qquad \beta:=s_2'-d_2 .$$
Then $1<p,q<\infty$, $\frac1p+\frac2q=3-(d_1+2d_2)<2$, $0<\alpha<2$, $0<\beta<1$ and $\alpha+2\beta=s'-(d_1+2d_2)>2$. By \eqref{bernsteinK} with these $p,q$, for every $f$,
\begin{equation}
\label{NKbound}
\begin{gathered}
N_{\alpha,\beta}(f;\mathcal{K})\lesssim\sum_{j,l\ge0}2^{(\alpha+d_1)j+(\beta+d_2)l}\|\Delta^x_j\Delta^y_lf\|_{L^1}=\|f\|_{B^{s_1',s_2'}_{1,1}},\\
N_{\alpha,\beta}(f;L^1)\le\|f\|_{B^{s_1',s_2'}_{1,1}} .
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Approximation. Let $f_0:=\langle X\rangle u_0$, which belongs to $B^{s_1,s_2}_{1,1}\subset B^{s_1',s_2'}_{1,1}$. By \eqref{NKbound} and Lemma \ref{lemmamixednorm} (i), $\|f_0\|_{\alpha,\beta;\mathcal{K}}+\|f_0\|_{\alpha,\beta;L^1}<\infty$; in particular $f_0\in L^1$. Let $u_{0,n}$ be the functions given by Lemma \ref{lemmaapprox} with $\theta=1$. By Lemma \ref{lemmaapprox} (i), $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $L^1\cap L^2$, and the first moments of $u_{0,n}$ are tight. Let $c\in\{\langle X\rangle^{-1},x\langle X\rangle^{-1},y\langle X\rangle^{-1}\}$. Since $\|c\,\mu_Z\|_{W^{3,\infty}}+\|\vartheta(\cdot/n)\|_{W^{3,\infty}}\lesssim1$ for $|Z|\le1$, the identity \eqref{weightconv}, Lemma \ref{lemmamixednorm} (ii), the invariance under translations and Minkowski's inequality give, for $Y\in\{L^1,\mathcal{K}\}$,
$$\|c\langle X\rangle u_{0,n}\|_{\alpha,\beta;Y}\le\sup_{|Z|\le1}\big\|c\,\mu_Z\,\tau_{-Z}\big(\vartheta(\cdot/n)f_0\big)\big\|_{\alpha,\beta;Y}\lesssim\|f_0\|_{\alpha,\beta;Y},$$
uniformly in $n$. Since $c\langle X\rangle\in\{1,x,y\}$, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemmamixed} hold.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Uniform asymptotics and identification of the state. By Lemma \ref{lemmamixed}, after extraction of a subsequence, the coefficients $a_n$ of $u_{0,n}$ satisfy \eqref{envelopemixed} and converge to a limit $a$ uniformly on the compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Each $a_n$ satisfies \eqref{hypa} by Proposition \ref{propdirect}, the function $F:=CF_{\alpha,\beta}$ satisfies \eqref{hypF1} and, by Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (i), the conditions \eqref{weightsF}, and the reconstructed functions $u_n$ are the solutions of \eqref{kp} with data $u_{0,n}$, by Corollary \ref{corsmooth}. Proposition \ref{propcone} gives \eqref{hypcone} with $g_n:=\mathcal{B} a_n$, for every compact set $V\subset\mathcal{V}$.
Lemma \ref{lemmasandwich}, applied with the majorant $F$, gives $\mathcal{B} a_n\to u_+:=\mathcal{B} a$ in $L^2$ and $\|u_+\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 4:} Conclusion. By the continuity of the $L^2$ flow \cite{Bourgain}, $u_n(t)\to u(t)$ in $L^2$ for every $t$, and $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|u_+\|_{L^2}$ by \eqref{mass}. Lemma \ref{lemmaweak} gives $\|u(t)-S(t)u_+\|_{L^2}\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ and as $t\to-\infty$. This proves Theorem \ref{thmmain} under condition (ii), with $u_+=u_-=\mathcal{B} a$.

body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Proof of (i). We decompose into the dyadic annuli $\{R\le|k-k_0|<2R\}$, which are contained in the discs $D(k_0,2R)$. By \eqref{potentialsets}, the potential of the indicator function of such an annulus is at most $4R$, so that a density $|k-k_0|^{-\gamma}$, $\gamma>0$, contributes at most $4R^{1-\gamma}$. Summing over the dyadic $R\in[\frac{r_1}2,r]$ for $\gamma=1$ (there are at most $2+\log_2\frac r{r_1}$ of them), and over the dyadic $R\ge\frac{r_1}2$ for $\gamma=2$, gives \eqref{annulusbound}. Summing over the dyadic $R\le r$ for $\gamma=\frac12$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{annulushalf}
\sup_{k\in\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{I}\big(|\cdot-k_0|^{-\frac12}\1_{D(k_0,r)}\big)(k)\lesssim r^{\frac12}.
\end{equation}

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} Proof of (ii). On $D_\pm$ we have $1+|k_2|\lesssim1$, and \eqref{propW} and \eqref{annulushalf} give
$$\int_{D_\pm}(1+|k_2|)W_t\,dA+\sup_{k\in\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{I}\big((1+|k_2|)W_t\1_{D_\pm}\big)(k)\lesssim\int_{D(0,r_0)}\frac{dA(z)}{|z|^{\frac12}}+r_0^{\frac12}\lesssim1 ,$$
and $1\le2^{\frac{3j}2}$. Outside $D_+\cup D_-$, \eqref{propW} gives $(1+|k_2|)W_t\lesssim(1+|k_2|)\langle k\rangle^{-\frac12}$. On $A_j$ we have $|k_2|<2^j$ and $|k_1|<\frac{2^j}{2|k_2|}$, since $|\zeta_2|=4|k_1k_2|<2^{j+1}$. For fixed $k_2$ with $|k_2|=s$, we use $\langle k\rangle\ge|k_1|$ and $\langle k\rangle\ge\max(1,s)$ to bound the integral in $k_1$:
$$\int_{\{|k_1|<\frac{2^j}{2s}\}}\langle k\rangle^{-\frac12}dk_1\le\min\Big(4\Big(\frac{2^j}{2s}\Big)^{\frac12},\ \frac{2^j}s\max(1,s)^{-\frac12}\Big).$$
We use the first bound for $s<2^{\frac j2}$ and the second one for $s\ge2^{\frac j2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{A_j}\frac{1+|k_2|}{\langle k\rangle^{\frac12}}\,dA&\lesssim\int_0^1\Big(\frac{2^j}s\Big)^{\frac12}ds+\int_1^{2^{j/2}}s\Big(\frac{2^j}s\Big)^{\frac12}ds+\int_{2^{j/2}}^{2^j}s\,\frac{2^j}{s^{\frac32}}\,ds\\&\lesssim2^{\frac j2}+2^{\frac{5j}4}+2^{\frac{3j}2}\lesssim2^{\frac{3j}2}.\end{aligned}$$
Moreover $(1+|k_2|)\langle k\rangle^{-\frac12}\le1+2^j\le2^{j+1}$ on $A_j$. By the last bound of \eqref{potentialsets}, the potential of $(1+|k_2|)W_t\1_{A_j\setminus(D_+\cup D_-)}$ is $O\big((2^j\cdot2^{\frac{3j}2})^{\frac12}\big)=O(2^{\frac{5j}4})$, hence $O(2^{\frac{3j}2})$ as well. This proves \eqref{shellbound}.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Proof of (iii). We use the rectangle bound of \eqref{potentialsets}. The rectangle $\{|k_1|<\varepsilon^{-1},\ |k_2|<\varepsilon\}$ has potential $O(\varepsilon\log\frac2\varepsilon)$. For $L=2^p\varepsilon^{-1}$, $p\ge0$, on $\{L\le|k_1|<2L,\ |k_2|<\varepsilon\}$ we have $\langle \zeta\rangle^{-\frac32}\le\langle 4Lk_2\rangle^{-\frac32}$; we split this set into $\{|k_2|<L^{-1}\}$, where the density is at most $1$, and the nonempty sets $\{2^{q-1}L^{-1}\le|k_2|<\min(2^qL^{-1},\varepsilon)\}$, $q\ge1$, where it is at most $2^{-\frac{3q}2}$. These are unions of four rectangles with sides $L$ and at most $2^{q+1}L^{-1}$, $q\ge0$, so that the potential of the density on $\{L\le|k_1|<2L,\ |k_2|<\varepsilon\}$ is at most
$$C\sum_{q=0}^{p}2^{-\frac{3q}2}\,\frac{2^{q+1}}L\Big(1+\log\frac{L^2}{2^{q}}\Big)\lesssim\frac{\log(2L)}L .$$
Summing over $p\ge0$ gives $O(\varepsilon\log\frac2\varepsilon)$, which proves the first bound of \eqref{stripbound}. For the second one, we bound $\langle k\rangle^{-2}$ by $L^{-2}$ on $\{L\le|k_1|<2L\}$, $L\ge1$ dyadic, and by $1$ on $\{|k_1|<1\}$; the corresponding sets are unions of at most two rectangles with sides at most $2L$ and $2\varepsilon$, and $\sum_{L}L^{-2}\varepsilon(1+\log\frac L\varepsilon)\lesssim\varepsilon\log\frac2\varepsilon$.

body_md:
{\bf Step 1:} Decomposition. Let $f_t:=\varrho_{1/|t|}\ast f$ be the average of $f$ at the scale $|t|^{-1}$. Since $\varrho$ is supported in the unit disc,
\begin{equation}
\label{averagef}
\|f-f_t\|_\infty\le|t|^{-\alpha}\|f\|_{C^\alpha},\qquad \|\nabla f_t\|_\infty\lesssim|t|^{1-\alpha}\|f\|_{C^\alpha},
\end{equation}
where for the second bound we write $\nabla f_t(k)=\int\nabla\varrho_{1/|t|}(k-k')(f(k')-f(k))\,dA(k')$. Let $c_{n,t}$ be defined as $c_n$, with $a_{n,t}$ in place of $a_n$. Since $\vartheta_t\Theta_t=0$, we have the decomposition
$$c_nPf=\Theta_tc_nPf+(1-\Theta_t)(c_n-c_{n,t})Pf+(1-\Theta_t)c_{n,t}(f-f_t)P+\vartheta_tc_{n,t}f_tP+wP,$$
with $w:=(1-\Theta_t)(1-\vartheta_t)c_{n,t}f_t$. Recall that $|\mathcal{C} g|\le\mathcal{I}|g|$. By \eqref{hypshell2} and Lemma \ref{lemmaregular} (i), $|c_n|+|c_{n,t}|\lesssim F_1$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} The terms without integration by parts. On the strip $\{|k_2|<2|t|^{-1}\}$ we have $F_1\lesssim\langle \zeta\rangle^{-\frac32}$, so that \eqref{stripbound} with $\varepsilon=2|t|^{-1}$ gives
$$\mathcal{I}|\Theta_tc_nPf|\lesssim\|f\|_\infty\,|t|^{-1}\log(2+|t|)\lesssim|t|^{-\frac12}\|f\|_\infty .$$
Since $|c_n-c_{n,t}|\le\mathcal E_{n,t}$ and $\sigma_t\le1$, \eqref{errorbounds} gives $\mathcal{I}|(1-\Theta_t)(c_n-c_{n,t})Pf|\le\|f\|_\infty\,\mathcal{I}\mathcal E_{n,t}\lesssim|t|^{-\frac12}\|f\|_\infty$. By \eqref{averagef} and the boundedness of $\mathcal{I} F_1$ (Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (i)), the third term has potential $O(|t|^{-\alpha}\|f\|_{C^\alpha})$. The fourth term is bounded by $C\|f\|_\infty$ and supported in $D(k_+,2\rho)\cup D(k_-,2\rho)$, so that its potential is at most $C\rho\|f\|_\infty$ by \eqref{potentialsets}.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Integration by parts. On the support of $w$ we have $|k-k_\pm|\ge\rho$, so that $\bar\partial\phi=\overline{\partial_k\phi}\neq0$. The function $w$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb{C}$, since it vanishes on the strip $\{|k_2|\le|t|^{-1}\}$, and $w/\bar\partial\phi\in C_0(\mathbb{C})$, since $w$ is bounded and $|\partial_k\phi|\gtrsim|t|\langle k\rangle^2$ outside $D_+\cup D_-$ (Lemma \ref{lemmaphase} (ii)). For fixed $n$, Lemma \ref{lemmaregular} (iii) shows that $w$ and $\bar\partial(w/\bar\partial\phi)$ are bounded and integrable, because $w$ vanishes on the strip $\{|k_2|\le|t|^{-1}\}$ and $\int_{\{|k_2|\ge|t|^{-1}\}}(1+|k_2|)\langle \zeta\rangle^{-6}\,dA<\infty$ by \eqref{changevariables}. Hence Lemma \ref{lemmacauchy} (vi), applied with $w$ in place of $f$, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{ibpcauchy}
\mathcal{C}(wP)=\frac{Pw}{i\bar\partial\phi}-\mathcal{C}\Big(P\,\bar\partial\Big(\frac w{i\bar\partial\phi}\Big)\Big).
\end{equation}
We now bound the right-hand side uniformly in $n$. By Lemma \ref{lemmaphase}, $|\partial_k\phi|\gtrsim|t||k-k_\pm|$ on $D_\pm$, $|\partial_k\phi|\gtrsim|t|\langle k\rangle^2$ outside $D_+\cup D_-$, and $|\partial_k^2\phi|\lesssim|t|\langle k\rangle$. First, by \eqref{propellt}, $|Pw/(i\bar\partial\phi)|\le\frac16\ell_t|w|\lesssim\rho\|f\|_\infty$. Next, since $\bar\partial^2\phi=\overline{\partial_k^2\phi}$,
$$\Big|\bar\partial\Big(\frac w{i\bar\partial\phi}\Big)\Big|\le\frac{|\nabla w|}{|\partial_k\phi|}+\frac{|w||\partial_k^2\phi|}{|\partial_k\phi|^2},$$
and $\nabla w$ is the sum of the terms where the derivative falls on $\Theta_t$, on $\vartheta_t$, on $a_{n,t}$, on $k_2$ (if $c_n=k_2a_n$) or on $f_t$. We bound the potentials of the corresponding densities.

The derivative of $\Theta_t$ is bounded by $C|t|$ and supported in $\{|t|^{-1}\le|k_2|\le2|t|^{-1}\}$, outside $D_+\cup D_-$, so that the corresponding density is bounded by $C\langle k\rangle^{-2}\1_{\{|k_2|\le2|t|^{-1}\}}\|f\|_\infty$. By \eqref{stripbound}, its potential is $O(|t|^{-1}\log(2+|t|)\|f\|_\infty)$. The derivative of $\vartheta_t$ is bounded by $C\rho^{-1}$ and supported in $D(k_\pm,2\rho)\setminus D(k_\pm,\rho)$, where $|\partial_k\phi|^{-1}\le\frac16\ell_t\lesssim\rho$ by \eqref{propellt}; the corresponding density is $O(\|f\|_\infty)$ on $D(k_\pm,2\rho)$, and its potential is $O(\rho\|f\|_\infty)$. The density produced by the derivative of $a_{n,t}$ is bounded by $\|f\|_\infty\mathcal E'_{n,t}$, whose potential is $O(|t|^{-\frac12}\sigma_t\|f\|_\infty)$ by \eqref{errorbounds}. By \eqref{averagef}, the densities produced by the derivatives of $f_t$ and of $k_2$ are bounded by $C|t|^{1-\alpha}\|f\|_{C^\alpha}(1-\vartheta_t)\frac{F_1}{|\partial_k\phi|}$, which is $O\big(|t|^{-\alpha}|k-k_\pm|^{-1}\big)\|f\|_{C^\alpha}$ on $D_\pm\setminus D(k_\pm,\rho)$, and $O\big(|t|^{-\alpha}F_1\langle k\rangle^{-2}\big)\|f\|_{C^\alpha}$ outside $D_+\cup D_-$. By \eqref{annulusbound}, and by the last bound of \eqref{potentialsets} together with $\int F_1\langle k\rangle^{-1}dA<\infty$ (Lemma \ref{lemmaweights} (i)), their potentials are $O(|t|^{-\alpha}\log(2+|t|)\|f\|_{C^\alpha})$. Finally, the density $\frac{|w||\partial_k^2\phi|}{|\partial_k\phi|^2}$ is $O\big(|t|^{-1}|k-k_\pm|^{-2}\|f\|_\infty\big)$ on $D_\pm\setminus D(k_\pm,\rho)$ and $O\big(|t|^{-1}F_1\langle k\rangle^{-3}\|f\|_\infty\big)$ outside $D_+\cup D_-$; by \eqref{annulusbound} and \eqref{potentialsets}, its potential is $O\big((|t|^{-1}\rho^{-1}+|t|^{-1})\|f\|_\infty\big)=O(\rho\|f\|_\infty)$.

Collecting Steps 2 and 3, and using $\rho=|t|^{-\frac12}$, $|t|^{-1}\log(2+|t|)\lesssim|t|^{-\frac12}$, $\sigma_t\le1$ and $|t|^{-\alpha}\log(2+|t|)\lesssim|t|^{-\frac12}$, which holds since $\alpha>\frac12$, we obtain \eqref{oschalf}.

Let $u_{0,n}$ be the functions of Lemma \ref{lemmahalfdirect}, so that $u_{0,n}\to u_0$ in $L^1\cap L^2$ by Lemma \ref{lemmaapprox} (i). By Lemma \ref{lemmahalfdirect} (ii), after extraction of a subsequence, the coefficients $a_n$ of $u_{0,n}$ converge to a limit $a$ uniformly on the compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 1:} Uniform asymptotics. Each $a_n$ satisfies \eqref{hypa} by Proposition \ref{propdirect}, and the function reconstructed from $a_n$ is the solution $u_n$ of \eqref{kp} with datum $u_{0,n}$, by Corollary \ref{corsmooth}. By Lemma \ref{lemmahalfdirect} (i) and Proposition \ref{propcritical}, \eqref{hypcone} holds with $g_n:=\mathcal{B} a_n$, for every compact set $V\subset\mathcal{V}$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 2:} The scattering state. By \eqref{hypshell2}, $|a_n|\le F=C_*\langle \zeta\rangle^{-\frac32}$ for every $n$, hence $|a|\le F$. By \eqref{changevariables},
$$8\int_\mathbb{C}|k_2|F(k)^2\,dA(k)=C_*^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\langle (\xi,\eta)\rangle^{-3}\,d\xi\,d\eta<\infty,$$
and the dominated convergence theorem gives $\|\mathcal{B} a_n-\mathcal{B} a\|_{L^2}^2=8\int|k_2||a_n-a|^2\,dA\to0$. By \eqref{plancherelsmooth}, $\|\mathcal{B} a_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_{0,n}\|_{L^2}\to\|u_0\|_{L^2}$. Hence $u_+:=\mathcal{B} a$ satisfies $\mathcal{B} a_n\to u_+$ in $L^2$ and $\|u_+\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}$.\\

\noindent{\bf Step 3:} Conclusion. The argument of Step 4 of the proof of Theorem \ref{thmmain} under condition (ii) applies without change: the continuity of the $L^2$ flow, \eqref{mass} and Lemma \ref{lemmaweak} give $\|u(t)-S(t)u_+\|_{L^2}\to0$ as $t\to\pm\infty$. This proves Theorem \ref{thmmain} under condition (i), with $u_+=u_-=\mathcal{B} a$.
